cards.front: Where the difficulty in live comments lies
cards.back: Not writes (about 11k a second) but knowing who is watching what as people scroll, and fanning out to huge audiences on a few hot streams.
About 11k a second; at about 1 KB each, roughly 40 GB an hour.
Subscription churn: viewers changing streams every ~100 s is about 500k watch or unwatch events a second, more than comments.

cards.front: Why polling fails at this scale
cards.back: 50M viewers polling every 5 s is 10M requests a second, nearly all 'nothing new', and comments still arrive 2.5 s late on average.
A stream's comments stay in order on one partition.

cards.front: Registry key: stream → gateways, not users
cards.back: At most about 500 entries per stream, updated only when a gateway's first viewer arrives or last one leaves. Most scrolling stays inside the gateway.
Gateways refresh entries while they have viewers; a crashed gateway's entries expire on their own and fan-out stops sending to it.
Each region keeps its own registry and gateways; comments are replicated to every region's Kafka and fanned out locally.

cards.front: Readable comment rate on a busy stream
cards.back: About 10 comments a second, ranked (friends first, then quality) and batched once a second. The rest are stored but not shown live.

cards.front: Why replication doesn't fix a hot registry key
cards.back: The problem is write volume and every replica takes every write. Coalescing updates and sub-sharding the key do help.
Append-only, read newest-first per stream, steady writes with spikes: leaderless, no primary to fail over, scales by adding nodes.

quiz.q: A World Cup stream has 1M viewers and 200 comments a second, and naive fan-out would be 200M pushes a second. What brings it down most?
choices: Replicate the registry
Rank to about 10 comments a second and batch once a second per gateway
Add more Kafka partitions
Switch to short polling
quiz.why: Ranking and batching bound fan-out by gateways, not comments.

quiz.q: The registry shard for a hot stream melts because every scroll writes a user ID to it. What redesign fixes this?
choices: Store stream → gateways and update only on a gateway's first or last viewer
Add read replicas
Store one big list value per stream
Move the registry to Cassandra
quiz.why: Keying by gateway keeps most scrolling inside the gateway.

quiz.q: A gateway crashes. Fan-out workers keep sending it comments for a while. What limits the damage?
choices: Fan-out workers ping each gateway first
Kafka retries
Registry entries expire by TTL since the gateway stops refreshing them
Clients poll instead
quiz.why: Expire, don't trust: dead gateways' entries vanish on their own.

quiz.q: Fan-out lags 30 seconds behind on a busy evening. What should it do?
choices: Deliver everything in order regardless of age
Pause commenting
Switch to cross-region lookups
Drop the oldest live deliveries first; they remain in history
quiz.why: A comment 30 s late is worse than one shown only in history.

quiz.q: Kafka goes down. What does the comment service do?
choices: Write straight to Cassandra and return success; live delivery pauses
Reject all comments
Buffer comments in gateway memory
Broadcast directly to all gateways
quiz.why: Live delivery can be best effort but the stored comment must not be lost.

quiz.q: A moderator hides an abusive comment already on viewers' screens. How is it removed?
choices: Clients poll for deletions every minute
A tombstone message travels the same fan-out path
The comment is deleted from Kafka
Gateways restart
quiz.why: Hides and deletes go out as tombstones so clients remove them.

quiz.q: A registry shard is lost. What keeps comments flowing until it's rebuilt?
choices: Nothing; those streams go silent
Viewers reconnect to a new region
Fan-out broadcasts those streams to all gateways in the region
Kafka holds them until the shard returns
quiz.why: Broadcasting costs more but delivers while gateways re-announce their streams.
